name: Transposed-letter effect
statement: A nonword made by swapping two letters of a word, such as jugde, activates that word far more strongly than a nonword made by replacing the same two letters.
meaning: The finding is about how the reading system codes where a letter sits, not about how easily jumbled prose can be read. In a masked-priming lexical decision task the prime flashes for about 40 to 50 milliseconds under a mask, too briefly to be reported, and the target follows in capitals. If uhser speeds the recognition of USHER more than ufner does, the two transposed letters are still doing lexical work in the wrong slots. That comparison is the whole experiment. Against an unrelated prime almost any partial overlap helps, so the control has to be a nonword that disturbs the same letter positions by substitution rather than by exchange. Models that give each letter its own position-specific channel predict no difference between the two, because in both primes the letters at those positions are wrong. The effect is the main reason such models were abandoned in favour of schemes that code relative position, among them Whitney's SERIOL bigrams, Davis's spatial coding and Grainger and van Heuven's open bigrams.

origin.who: Kenneth I. Forster, Chris Davis, Carole Schoknecht and Rosemarie Carter
origin.where: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology Section A
origin.note: Their paper "Masked priming with graphemically related forms: Repetition or partial activation?" contains the first masked-priming test with transposed primes. Perea and Lupker name Bruner and O'Dowd (1958), Chambers (1979) and O'Connor and Forster (1981) as earlier evidence that transposed-letter nonwords resemble their base words, and the label came from later authors.

evidence: Perea and Lupker summarise Experiment 1 of Forster and colleagues as follows: six-letter targets, a 60 ms prime-target interval, and mean latencies of 486 ms for identity primes (sailor-SAILOR), 487 ms for transposed-letter primes (salior-SAILOR), 500 ms for one-letter-different primes (sanlor-SAILOR) and 550 ms for unrelated words (cheese-SAILOR). Those figures are quoted here from Perea and Lupker's table rather than read off the 1987 paper. Perea and Lupker then supplied the orthographic control the earlier work lacked, in three experiments at the University of Western Ontario with a 40 ms prime and a 40 ms mask. Experiment 1 used 36 students and 120 five-letter targets. Primes with two internal letters exchanged (uhser-USHER, 556 ms) beat their substitution control (ufner-USHER, 586 ms) by 30 ms, F(1,30) = 18.92, p < .001, while primes with the last two letters exchanged (ushre-USHER, 554 ms) beat ushno-USHER (567 ms) by 13 ms, F(1,30) = 3.53, p < .07. Identity primes were worth 47 ms. Experiment 2 used 30 students and added unrelated baselines: 22 ms for internal transpositions, F(1,24) = 11.77, p < .001, and 11 ms for final ones, F(1,24) = 2.42, p > .10. Experiment 3 used 32 students and 160 six-letter targets, giving 44 ms for internal transpositions, F(1,24) = 85.19, p < .001, and 12 ms for final ones, F(1,24) = 4.27, p = .05. Measured instead against unrelated controls the two came out at 44 and 39 ms, and the authors say the internal advantage rests on the internal substitution control being slow rather than on the transposed prime being fast. The letters need not be neighbours. In Spanish, Perea and Lupker found that caniso primed CASINO 21 ms faster than caviro did, F1(1,24) = 13.00, with 28 students, and 17 ms faster in a second group of 28, F1(1,24) = 7.47. Vowels behaved differently: with 24 students, anamil-ANIMAL came out 9 ms slower than anomel-ANIMAL, and with 62 students and words of seven to ten letters the consonant effect was 18 ms, F1(1,60) = 32.29, against 6 ms for vowels, F1(1,60) = 2.19, p > .10, interaction F1(1,60) = 4.37.

replication.headline: A 14-site study of over 1,000 readers put medial transposed-letter priming at 31.42 ms, in an experiment precise enough to call 2.90 ms reliable.
replication.detail: Adelman and 17 co-authors built the Form Priming Project to settle exactly this kind of comparison. Over 1,000 participants at 14 university sites each did 840 trials of primed lexical decision across 28 prime types on the same 420 six-letter word targets. Tukey's HSD on their estimate of the error term makes a 2.90 ms difference between conditions reliable at 5%, 3.24 ms at 1% and 3.66 ms at 0.1%. Against the arbitrary unrelated prime at 677.17 ms, identity primes gained 42.69 ms. The three transposition conditions came next after identity and the two single-letter deletions: final transpositions (desing-DESIGN) 32.46 ms, medial transpositions (desgin-DESIGN) 31.42 ms, initial transpositions (edsign-DESIGN) 29.03 ms. Medial substitution of the same two letters gained 22.68 ms and double medial substitution 14.94 ms, so transposition beat replacement, as earlier work had reported. A prime keeping only the two exterior letters (dzbtkn-DESIGN) gained 2.34 ms and a reversal of everything after the first letter (dngise-DESIGN) 2.86 ms, both below the unrelated pseudoword baseline. The authors also report small but reliable priming from extreme transpositions that earlier studies had recorded as null, including 16.77 ms from edisng-DESIGN and 8.80 ms from igndes-DESIGN, and they attribute the discrepancy to power or to the greater length of the earlier stimuli. Their initial-versus-final ordering does not match Schoonbaert and Grainger's French result, and they say so.

replicated.unit: ms of lexical decision latency, medial transposed-letter prime against an arbitrary unrelated prime

limits: The effect is not a property of alphabets in general. Velan and Frost gave Hebrew readers masked primes formed by transposing two letters of a word's consonantal root, in three lexical decision experiments with 51, 80 and 84 students. Root primes helped, by 21 and 18 ms in Experiment 1. Transposed-root primes hurt: 14 and 10 ms of inhibition in Experiment 1, 9 ms in Experiment 2, and 11 ms in Experiment 3 where identity primes were worth 29 ms. Their conclusion is that a Hebrew root with two letters swapped is a different root, and it recruits the wrong family of words. Perea, abu Mallouh and Carreiras found the same split in Arabic. With 26 students at the University of Amman, primes transposing two root letters produced nothing at all, at minus 1, minus 4 and minus 6 ms across initial, middle and final positions. With 28 students, primes that transposed a root letter with a word-pattern letter, leaving root order intact, produced 16 ms. The boundary is morphological rather than genealogical. Perea, Gatt, Moret-Tatay and Fabri ran the sentence task in Maltese, a Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet with its vowels spelled out and a productive Romance morphology alongside its root-and-pattern one. Twenty students at the University of Malta reproduced target words with two root letters transposed as often as intact ones, 81.5% against 81.0% in Maltese and 76.5% against 78.0% in English, all Fs < 1. Within English the effect also depends on what is moved: Perea and Lupker's vowel transpositions produced nothing, and transposing the final two letters is worth roughly a third of transposing two internal ones.
misreadings: The famous version of this effect is an email, and the email is not a study. It circulated from September 2003 and claimed that Cambridge University research had shown letter order does not matter provided the first and last letters stay put. Matt Davis at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, who first heard of it when a journalist approached his colleague Sian Miller on 16 September, writes that "there's no-one in Cambridge UK who is currently doing research on this topic". The nearest real antecedent he traces is Graham Rawlinson's unpublished 1976 Nottingham doctoral thesis, "The significance of letter position in word recognition", which Rawlinson described in a 1999 letter to New Scientist as showing that randomising letters in the middle of words had little or no effect on skilled readers. Davis lists what makes the demonstration text easy: short words and function words do not change at all, 8 of the 15 words in its first sentence are in the correct order, the transpositions are adjacent, none of them creates another word, they preserve the sound of the original, and the passage is predictable. Grainger and Whitney, who used the email to introduce open-bigram coding, put it at almost 50% of words unscrambled. The claim that jumbled text costs nothing is false. The unit's page on the email reports Rayner and colleagues' eye-tracking result that "the reading rate decreased by 11% for sentences containing words with word-internal transpositions and by 36% and 26% when transpositions were at the beginnings or ends, respectively", a figure quoted here from that page rather than from the 2006 paper. The laboratory effect is a matter of milliseconds in a masked comparison, and it says that letter position is coded loosely, not that it is ignored.
